Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 107, verses 4–5:

Imam Ahmad said: "They used to delay it until its time had passed."

(Section)

Neglecting the prayer (al-sahw 'anha) does not mean abandoning it, for otherwise they would not be described as people who pray. It is rather neglect of its obligations, either neglect of its proper time, as Ibn Mas'ud and others said, or neglect of presence of heart and humility (al-khushu'). The correct view is that it includes both kinds. Allah, glory be to Him, affirmed that they performed a prayer and described them as neglectful of it. This means neglect of its obligatory time, or neglect of its sincerity and its obligatory presence of heart. For this reason He described them as showing off (al-riya'), and if the neglect were neglect of abandonment, there would be no showing off.

They said: Even if we assume it is neglect of an obligation only, the threat of woe (wayl) is then a pointer, by a stronger inference, to the threat against neglecting sincerity and presence of heart, for several reasons. The first: the time (of the prayer) falls away in cases of excuse and is replaced by a substitute, whereas sincerity and presence of heart never fall away in any circumstance and have no substitute.

The second: the obligation of the time is waived to complete the benefit of presence of heart. Thus it is permitted to combine two prayers because of a preoccupation that prevents performing one of them at its time without attention and presence of heart, such as the traveler, the sick person, and the one with an occupation that requires combining, as Ahmad and others stated explicitly.

In sum: the benefit of sincerity and presence of heart, and the gathering of the heart upon Allah in prayer, outweighs in the view of the Lawgiver the benefit of all its other obligations. How then could one think that He would invalidate it by omitting one takbir, or the proper rising from bowing in a pillar (rukn), or omitting a letter or a shaddah of the Qur'an, or omitting a tasbih, or the saying "Allah hears those who praise Him," or "Our Lord, and to You belongs praise," or the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by invoking blessings upon him, and then declare it valid while its essence, its greatest purpose, its spirit and its secret are lost?

This is the argument that this group relied upon, and as you see, these are arguments of considerable strength and clarity.

He said in (al-Salah wa Ahkam Tarikiha, "The Prayer and the Rulings on One Who Abandons It"):

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So woe to the worshippers who are heedless of their prayer.﴾

The early scholars differed about the meaning of heedlessness regarding it. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Masruq ibn al-Ajda' and others said that it is abandoning it until its time has passed.

A prophetic report (marfu') has been related on this. Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi said: Sufyan ibn Abi Shaybah related to us, 'Ikrimah ibn Ibrahim related to us, 'Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr related to us, from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, from his father, that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about "those who are heedless of their prayer," and he said: "They are those who delay the prayer beyond its time."

Hammad ibn Zayd said: 'Asim related to us, from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd, who said: "I said to my father: O father, what do you think of the saying of Allah: ﴿Those who are heedless of their prayer⦆? Which of us does not forget? Which of us does not let his mind wander?" He said: "It is not that; rather it is wasting the time (of the prayer)."

(Sunan al-Bayhaqi)

Haywah ibn Shurayh said: Abu Sakhr informed me that he asked Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi about the saying of Allah: ﴿Those who are heedless of their prayer⦆. He said: "It is one who abandons it." Then he asked him about al-Ma'un (small kindnesses), and he said: "Withholding wealth from its due."

Having established this, the threat of woe has been applied in the Qur'an to disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿Woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat and who are disbelievers in the Hereafter.⦆ And His saying: ﴿Woe to every lying sinner, who hears the verses of Allah recited to him, then persists arrogantly as though he had not heard them. So give him the tidings of a painful punishment. And when he learns anything of Our verses, he takes them in mockery. For such there is a humiliating punishment.⦆ And His saying: ﴿And woe to the disbelievers from a severe punishment.⦆ The exception is two places: ﴿Woe to the defrauders⦆ and ﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter⦆. Here woe is linked to defrauding, and to slander and backbiting, and these do not by themselves make one a disbeliever. So the woe of one who abandons the prayer is either to be counted with the woe of disbelievers or with the woe of sinners (fussaq). Counting it with the woe of disbelievers is more fitting, for two reasons:

The first: it is authentically reported from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas concerning this verse that he said: "If they had abandoned it, they would be disbelievers; but they neglected its time."

The second: the proofs we will mention for his disbelief, which clarify it. The fifth proof is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires, so they will encounter error (ghayy).⦆

Shu'bah ibn al-Hajjaj said: Abu Ishaq related to us, from Abu 'Ubaydah, from 'Abd Allah, that is Ibn Mas'ud, concerning this verse, that he said: "It is a river in Hell, foul in taste, deep in its bottom."

Muhammad ibn Nasr said: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Ibrahim related to us, Muhammad ibn Ziyad ibn Zabbar related to us, Sharqi ibn al-Qatami related to me, who said: Luqman ibn 'Amir al-Khuza'i related to me, who said: I went to Abu Umamah al-Bahili and said: "Tell me a hadith you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'If a rock were hurled from the edge of Hell, it would not reach its bottom in seventy autumns. Then it would reach ghayy and athām.'" I said: "What are ghayy and athām?" He said: "Two wells at the bottom of Hell, into which flows the pus of the people of Hell. This is what Allah mentioned in His Book": ﴿so they will encounter ghayy⦆ and ﴿athām⦆.

Muhammad ibn Nasr said: al-Hasan ibn 'Isa related to us, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak related to us, Hushaym ibn Bashir informed us, who said: Zakariyya ibn Abi Maryam al-Khuza'i informed me, who said: I heard Abu Umamah al-Bahili say: "The distance between the edge of Hell and its bottom is a journey of fifty autumns, of a stone that falls, or he said a rock that plunges, its size like ten great fat cauldrons."

A mawla of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Khalid ibn al-Walid then said to him: "Is there anything beneath that, O Abu Umamah?" He said: "Yes, ghayy and athām." Ayyub ibn Bashir related from Shafi ibn Mati', who said: "In Hell there is a valley called ghayy, which flows with blood and pus, and it is for those created for it." Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿so they will encounter ghayy⦆.

The point of the inference from the verse is that Allah, glory be to Him, made this place of the Fire for one who neglects the prayer and follows his desires. Had he been among the sinful Muslims, they would be in the upper levels of the Fire, not in this place, which is its lowest part, for this is not a dwelling of the people of Islam but of the disbelievers.

There is another proof in the verse, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they will encounter ghayy, except those who repent, believe, and do righteous deeds⦆. Had the one who neglects the prayer been a believer, repentance would not have been conditioned upon faith, and that would be obtaining what is already obtained.

**(Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, on Surah 107, verses 6–7, part 1 of 2)**

It has been said regarding His words, ﴿and withhold small kindnesses﴾, that they are the cooking pot, the axe, and the bowl.

*Al-ma'un* is a comprehensive term for everything from which one benefits. Some of the early generation (*salaf*) mentioned these examples to the questioner by way of illustration and to draw attention, from the lesser to the greater.

**(An admonition)**

Do not ride, though you have no camel. Do not draw a bow, though you have no string.

How many have spent their souls in showing off, so that people would praise them; their souls were lost, and the praise turned into blame. Had they spent them for God, they would have remained as long as time endures.

[Surah al-Ma'un]

The work of the show-off is like a prayer made entirely of husks.

The show-off fills his provision bag with sand, which weighs him down on the road and benefits him not.

The scent of showing off is a carrion; the nostrils of hearts turn away from it.

When the silkworm began to weave, the spider came and resembled it, saying: "You weave, and I weave too." The silkworm replied: "My weaving is the robes of kings, and your weaving is a net for flies." And at the touch of need, the difference becomes clear.

*(Poetry)*
When tears mingle on the cheeks,
the one who truly weeps is distinguished from the one who feigns weeping.

The pine tree bears fruit after thirty years, while the gourd tree climbs up in two weeks. The gourd says to the pine seedling: "The road you covered in thirty years, I covered in two weeks. It is said, 'You have a tree, and I have a tree.'" The pine replied to it: "Wait, until the autumn winds blow. If it (your tree) stands firm, then your boast is complete."

Sufism and poverty used to dwell in the places of the hearts; now they have become outward garments. It was a patched cloak, and it has become a trade.

Change your attire, O show-off, for it will say to you: "Leave me, and take me."

The sword and the shield are for adorning your appearance; but the fraud of counterfeit gold is revealed at the test.

If you had seen the vanguard of the sincere (*siddiqin*) at the front of the caravan, or heard the cries for help of the lovers in the middle of the caravan, or witnessed the rear-guard of those who seek forgiveness at the back of the caravan, you would have known that you have been cut off beneath the tree of Umm Ghaylan.

Alas for the one cut off, left behind the caravan, counting the stations!

**[Section: On giving and generosity]**

If it is supposed that a group of people are compelled to dwell in a person's house, having no other place, or to lodge in a privately owned inn, or to borrow clothes with which to warm themselves, or a millstone for grinding, or a bucket for drawing water, or a pot, or an axe, or something else of the kind: then it is obligatory upon its owner to lend it, without dispute. But may he take a fee for it? On this there are two opinions among the scholars, and these are two positions within the school of Ahmad.

Whoever permits taking a fee forbids him to demand more than the customary wage (*ujrat al-mithl*).

Our Shaykh said: "The correct view is that it is obligatory to give this without payment, as the Book and the Sunnah indicate. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show of their deeds, and withhold small kindnesses﴾."

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others among the Companions said: "It is lending the cooking pot, the bucket, the axe, and the like."

In the *Two Sahihs* (Bukhari and Muslim), from the Prophet (ﷺ), when he mentioned horses, he said: "For one man they are a reward, for another a covering, and for another a burden. As for the one for whom they are a reward: a man who tied them in the way of God. As for the one for whom they are a covering: a man who tied them out of self-sufficiency and chastity, and did not forget God's right concerning their necks or their backs."

In the *Two Sahihs*, also from him: "Among the rights of camels is lending their bucket and stallion for service."

In the *Two Sahihs*, from him: "He forbade the payment for stud service (*'asb al-fahl*)." That is, he forbade taking a fee for it, though people need it. Thus he made giving it freely obligatory, and forbade taking a fee for it.

In the *Two Sahihs*, from him, he said: "Let no neighbour prevent his neighbour from fixing a beam into his wall."

If someone needs to channel his water through another's land, without harm to the landowner, is he to be compelled to do so? There are two narrations from Ahmad. Compulsion is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and others among the Companions, may God be pleased with them all.

A group of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'in*) said: "The zakat on jewelry is its lending. So if one does not lend it, then its zakat must be paid." This is a position in the school of Ahmad. I say: this is the preponderant view, and jewelry is never free of either zakat or lending.

The benefits that must be given are of two kinds. Among them is that which is a right of property, as we mentioned concerning horses, camels, and jewelry. Among them is that which is required by people's need.

Moreover, the giving of the benefits of the body becomes obligatory when there is need, such as teaching knowledge, giving legal opinions to people, judging between them, giving testimony, jihad, commanding good and forbidding evil, and other benefits of the body. Likewise, whoever is able to rescue a person from destruction is obliged to save him; if he abandons that while able to do it, he sins and is liable for it.

So there is no barrier to the obligation of giving the benefits of property to the one in need. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and He said: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as God has taught him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

On taking a fee (*ju'l*) for testimony, the jurists have four opinions, and these are four positions in the school of Ahmad. One of them: it is not permitted at all. The second: it is permitted when there is need. The third: it is not permitted unless it becomes obligatory for him. The fourth: it is permitted, but if he takes it at the time of bearing the testimony, he does not take it at the time of delivering it.

The intent is this: what the Prophet (ﷺ) determined as the price in the case of partial manumission (*sirayat al-'itq*) was for the completion of freedom, which is a right of God. And what people need in a general way, the right in it belongs to God. This applies to the rights and the prescribed penalties (*hudud*). As for the rights, they are like the rights of the mosques, the property of *fay'* (booty without battle), endowments (*waqf*) for those in need, the wealth of charity, and public benefits.

As for the prescribed penalties, they are like the penalty for armed robbery (*muharabah*), theft, fornication, and drinking intoxicants.

The Muslims' need for food, clothing, and other things is a general interest, in which the right does not belong to any single person. Therefore, fixing the price for it at the customary price upon the one obliged to sell is more appropriate than fixing it for the completion of freedom. Yet the completion of freedom is obligatory upon the partner who frees the slave; if no price were fixed for it, the other partner would be harmed by his demanding whatever he wished. Here, however, the general public buys food and clothing for themselves and others. If whoever has goods that people need were permitted to sell at whatever price he pleased, the harm to people would be greater. For this reason the jurists said: if a person is compelled to the food of another, the other must give it to him at the customary price.

The imam furthest from requiring exchange and fixing its price is al-Shafi'i. Nevertheless, he obliges whoever is compelled by a person's need for his food to give it to him at the customary price. His followers disputed the permissibility of fixing the price of food when people are in need of it, and they have two positions on this.

The companions of Abu Hanifa said: "It is not appropriate for the ruler to fix prices for the people, except when the harm to the public is involved. When the matter is referred to the judge, he orders the hoarder (*muhtakir*) to sell what exceeds his own and his family's subsistence, at the prevailing price in that regard, and forbids him from hoarding. If he refuses, he detains him and disciplines him as his judgment deems fit, as a deterrent to him and to prevent harm to the people." They said: "If the owners of food transgress and exceed the value grossly, and the judge is unable to protect the rights of the Muslims except by fixing prices, then he fixes them at that point, by consultation with the people of opinion and insight."

This is clearly consistent with the principle of Abu Hanifa, since he does not consider a free person to be restricted. Whoever sells to them at the price determined by the ruler is valid, because he was not coerced into it.

They said: "Does the judge sell the hoarder's food without his consent? This is subject to the well-known disagreement concerning the sale of a debtor's property. It is said that here he sells by consensus, because Abu Hanifa considers restriction (*hajr*) to remove general harm."

When prices rose during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and they asked him to fix prices, he refused. It is not reported that there was anyone there who had food and withheld it from sale. Rather, most of those who sold food were importers (*jallabun*) who sold when they came down to the market. But the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade "that a town-dweller sell for a desert-dweller" (*an yabi'a hadir li-badin*), that is, that a town-dweller act as a broker (*simsar*) for him.

He also said: "Leave people, God gives provision to some of them from others." So he forbade the townsman who knew the price from acting as agent for the desert-dweller who brought the goods, because when he acts as agent for him, despite his knowledge of people's need, he raises the price for the buyer. He forbade acting as agent for him, though the kind of agency is permissible, because of what it entails of raising prices upon the people. He also forbade intercepting the caravans (*talaqqi al-jalab*), and made it the seller's option (*khiyar*) when he comes down to the market. For this reason most jurists hold that he forbade it because of the harm it causes to the seller here: if he has not known the price, and the intercepting party meets him before he comes to the market, the buyer purchases from him below the customary price and cheats him. So the Prophet (ﷺ) established the option of this seller.

Then, concerning this, there are two narrations from Ahmad, as already mentioned. One: the option is established for him absolutely, whether he was cheated or not, and this is the apparent position of al-Shafi'i. The second: it is established only when he has been cheated, and this is the apparent position of the school.

Another group said: "Rather, he forbade it because of the harm to the buyer if the intercepting party meets him and buys from him, then sells it." In general, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade buying and selling whose kind is lawful, until the seller knows the price, which is the customary price, and the buyer knows the commodity.

The one who holds corrupt analogy (*qiyas fasid*) says: "The buyer may buy wherever he wishes, and he has bought from the seller, just as he says that he may act as agent for the resident seller and the non-resident seller." But the Lawgiver took into account the general interest, for if the importer does not know the price, he is ignorant of the customary price, so the buyer becomes a deceiver to him. Malik and Ahmad extended this to every *mustarsil* (one who is easily taken in in trade), for he is like the ignorant importer who does not know the price.

Thus it is clear that a person is obliged not to sell to such people except at the known price, which is the customary price, even if they are not in need of buying from him, because they are ignorant of the value, or do not bargain. Sale requires consent, and consent follows knowledge. Whoever does not know that it is a cheat may consent or may not consent. But if he knows that it is a cheat and consents, then there is no harm in it.

In the *Sunan* (of Abu Dawud): "A man had a tree on the land of another, and the landowner was harmed by the entry of the tree's owner. He complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), who commanded him to accept its exchange or to give it to him as a gift. He did not do so. So he permitted the landowner to uproot it, and said to the owner of the tree: 'You are only a harmer.'"

The one who holds corrupt analogy says: "He is not obliged to sell his tree, nor to give it away as a gift, nor is it permissible for the landowner to uproot it, because that is a disposal of another's property without his permission, and compulsion to exchange it." But the Lawgiver obliged him, if he would not give it as a gift, to sell it, because in that is the benefit of the landowner in being freed from the harm of the tree owner's entry, and the benefit of the tree owner in taking its value. Even if there is a slight harm to him in that, the harm to the landowner from its remaining in his orchard is greater. The Wise Lawgiver averts the greater of two harms by the lesser of them. This is jurisprudence, analogy, and the public interest, whoever refuses it.

The intent is this: this is evidence for the obligation of selling when the buyer is in need. And where is this from the general need of people for food and other things? The ruling on exchange of benefits, when people are in need of them, such as the benefit of houses, grinding, baking, and the like, is the ruling on exchange of goods.

The sum of the matter is this: when the people's interest cannot be completed except by fixing prices, then the ruler fixes prices for them at a just price, neither deficient nor excessive. And when their need is met and their interest is established without it, he does not do so. And success is from God.

**[Section: On the causes for which the people of the graves are punished]**

This is the question of the questioner: What are the causes for which the people of the graves are punished?

Its answer is given from two aspects: a summary (*mujmal*) and a detailed account (*mufassal*).

As for the summary: they are punished for their ignorance of God, their neglect of His command, and their committing of His prohibitions. God does not punish a soul that knew Him, loved Him, obeyed His command, and avoided His prohibition, nor a body that was ever in obedience. those who build mosques over graves and light lamps and lanterns upon them; those who give short measure, taking full measure for themselves when they receive, and diminishing what is owed when they give; the tyrants and the arrogant; the showoffs, the slanderers, the defamers, and those who revile the predecessors; those who go to soothsayers, astrologers and diviners, ask them and believe them; the helpers of oppressors who have sold their hereafter for the worldly gain of others; **(Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, on Surah 107, verses 6–7, part 1 of 2)**

It has been said regarding His words, ﴿and withhold small kindnesses﴾, that they are the cooking pot, the axe, and the bowl.

*Al-ma'un* is a comprehensive term for everything from which one benefits. Some of the early generation (*salaf*) mentioned these examples to the questioner by way of illustration and to draw attention, from the lesser to the greater.

**(An admonition)**

Do not ride, though you have no camel. Do not draw a bow, though you have no string.

How many have spent their souls in showing off, so that people would praise them; their souls were lost, and the praise turned into blame. Had they spent them for God, they would have remained as long as time endures.

[Surah al-Ma'un]

The work of the show-off is like a prayer made entirely of husks.

The show-off fills his provision bag with sand, which weighs him down on the road and benefits him not.

The scent of showing off is a carrion; the nostrils of hearts turn away from it.

When the silkworm began to weave, the spider came and resembled it, saying: "You weave, and I weave too." The silkworm replied: "My weaving is the robes of kings, and your weaving is a net for flies." And at the touch of need, the difference becomes clear.

*(Poetry)*
When tears mingle on the cheeks,
the one who truly weeps is distinguished from the one who feigns weeping.

The pine tree bears fruit after thirty years, while the gourd tree climbs up in two weeks. The gourd says to the pine seedling: "The road you covered in thirty years, I covered in two weeks. It is said, 'You have a tree, and I have a tree.'" The pine replied to it: "Wait, until the autumn winds blow. If it (your tree) stands firm, then your boast is complete."

Sufism and poverty used to dwell in the places of the hearts; now they have become outward garments. It was a patched cloak, and it has become a trade.

Change your attire, O show-off, for it will say to you: "Leave me, and take me."

The sword and the shield are for adorning your appearance; but the fraud of counterfeit gold is revealed at the test.

If you had seen the vanguard of the sincere (*siddiqin*) at the front of the caravan, or heard the cries for help of the lovers in the middle of the caravan, or witnessed the rear-guard of those who seek forgiveness at the back of the caravan, you would have known that you have been cut off beneath the tree of Umm Ghaylan.

Alas for the one cut off, left behind the caravan, counting the stations!

**[Section: On giving and generosity]**

If it is supposed that a group of people are compelled to dwell in a person's house, having no other place, or to lodge in a privately owned inn, or to borrow clothes with which to warm themselves, or a millstone for grinding, or a bucket for drawing water, or a pot, or an axe, or something else of the kind: then it is obligatory upon its owner to lend it, without dispute. But may he take a fee for it? On this there are two opinions among the scholars, and these are two positions within the school of Ahmad.

Whoever permits taking a fee forbids him to demand more than the customary wage (*ujrat al-mithl*).

Our Shaykh said: "The correct view is that it is obligatory to give this without payment, as the Book and the Sunnah indicate. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Woe to those who pray, who are heedless of their prayer, who make show of their deeds, and withhold small kindnesses﴾."

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and others among the Companions said: "It is lending the cooking pot, the bucket, the axe, and the like."

In the *Two Sahihs* (Bukhari and Muslim), from the Prophet (ﷺ), when he mentioned horses, he said: "For one man they are a reward, for another a covering, and for another a burden. As for the one for whom they are a reward: a man who tied them in the way of God. As for the one for whom they are a covering: a man who tied them out of self-sufficiency and chastity, and did not forget God's right concerning their necks or their backs."

In the *Two Sahihs*, also from him: "Among the rights of camels is lending their bucket and stallion for service."

In the *Two Sahihs*, from him: "He forbade the payment for stud service (*'asb al-fahl*)." That is, he forbade taking a fee for it, though people need it. Thus he made giving it freely obligatory, and forbade taking a fee for it.

In the *Two Sahihs*, from him, he said: "Let no neighbour prevent his neighbour from fixing a beam into his wall."

If someone needs to channel his water through another's land, without harm to the landowner, is he to be compelled to do so? There are two narrations from Ahmad. Compulsion is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and others among the Companions, may God be pleased with them all.

A group of the Companions and the Successors (*tabi'in*) said: "The zakat on jewelry is its lending. So if one does not lend it, then its zakat must be paid." This is a position in the school of Ahmad. I say: this is the preponderant view, and jewelry is never free of either zakat or lending.

The benefits that must be given are of two kinds. Among them is that which is a right of property, as we mentioned concerning horses, camels, and jewelry. Among them is that which is required by people's need.

Moreover, the giving of the benefits of the body becomes obligatory when there is need, such as teaching knowledge, giving legal opinions to people, judging between them, giving testimony, jihad, commanding good and forbidding evil, and other benefits of the body. Likewise, whoever is able to rescue a person from destruction is obliged to save him; if he abandons that while able to do it, he sins and is liable for it.

So there is no barrier to the obligation of giving the benefits of property to the one in need. God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282], and He said: ﴿And let not a scribe refuse to write as God has taught him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282].

On taking a fee (*ju'l*) for testimony, the jurists have four opinions, and these are four positions in the school of Ahmad. One of them: it is not permitted at all. The second: it is permitted when there is need. The third: it is not permitted unless it becomes obligatory for him. The fourth: it is permitted, but if he takes it at the time of bearing the testimony, he does not take it at the time of delivering it.

The intent is this: what the Prophet (ﷺ) determined as the price in the case of partial manumission (*sirayat al-'itq*) was for the completion of freedom, which is a right of God. And what people need in a general way, the right in it belongs to God. This applies to the rights and the prescribed penalties (*hudud*). As for the rights, they are like the rights of the mosques, the property of *fay'* (booty without battle), endowments (*waqf*) for those in need, the wealth of charity, and public benefits.

As for the prescribed penalties, they are like the penalty for armed robbery (*muharabah*), theft, fornication, and drinking intoxicants.

The Muslims' need for food, clothing, and other things is a general interest, in which the right does not belong to any single person. Therefore, fixing the price for it at the customary price upon the one obliged to sell is more appropriate than fixing it for the completion of freedom. Yet the completion of freedom is obligatory upon the partner who frees the slave; if no price were fixed for it, the other partner would be harmed by his demanding whatever he wished. Here, however, the general public buys food and clothing for themselves and others. If whoever has goods that people need were permitted to sell at whatever price he pleased, the harm to people would be greater. For this reason the jurists said: if a person is compelled to the food of another, the other must give it to him at the customary price.

The imam furthest from requiring exchange and fixing its price is al-Shafi'i. Nevertheless, he obliges whoever is compelled by a person's need for his food to give it to him at the customary price. His followers disputed the permissibility of fixing the price of food when people are in need of it, and they have two positions on this.

The companions of Abu Hanifa said: "It is not appropriate for the ruler to fix prices for the people, except when the harm to the public is involved. When the matter is referred to the judge, he orders the hoarder (*muhtakir*) to sell what exceeds his own and his family's subsistence, at the prevailing price in that regard, and forbids him from hoarding. If he refuses, he detains him and disciplines him as his judgment deems fit, as a deterrent to him and to prevent harm to the people." They said: "If the owners of food transgress and exceed the value grossly, and the judge is unable to protect the rights of the Muslims except by fixing prices, then he fixes them at that point, by consultation with the people of opinion and insight."

This is clearly consistent with the principle of Abu Hanifa, since he does not consider a free person to be restricted. Whoever sells to them at the price determined by the ruler is valid, because he was not coerced into it.

They said: "Does the judge sell the hoarder's food without his consent? This is subject to the well-known disagreement concerning the sale of a debtor's property. It is said that here he sells by consensus, because Abu Hanifa considers restriction (*hajr*) to remove general harm."

When prices rose during the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and they asked him to fix prices, he refused. It is not reported that there was anyone there who had food and withheld it from sale. Rather, most of those who sold food were importers (*jallabun*) who sold when they came down to the market. But the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade "that a town-dweller sell for a desert-dweller" (*an yabi'a hadir li-badin*), that is, that a town-dweller act as a broker (*simsar*) for him.

He also said: "Leave people, God gives provision to some of them from others." So he forbade the townsman who knew the price from acting as agent for the desert-dweller who brought the goods, because when he acts as agent for him, despite his knowledge of people's need, he raises the price for the buyer. He forbade acting as agent for him, though the kind of agency is permissible, because of what it entails of raising prices upon the people. He also forbade intercepting the caravans (*talaqqi al-jalab*), and made it the seller's option (*khiyar*) when he comes down to the market. For this reason most jurists hold that he forbade it because of the harm it causes to the seller here: if he has not known the price, and the intercepting party meets him before he comes to the market, the buyer purchases from him below the customary price and cheats him. So the Prophet (ﷺ) established the option of this seller.

Then, concerning this, there are two narrations from Ahmad, as already mentioned. One: the option is established for him absolutely, whether he was cheated or not, and this is the apparent position of al-Shafi'i. The second: it is established only when he has been cheated, and this is the apparent position of the school.

Another group said: "Rather, he forbade it because of the harm to the buyer if the intercepting party meets him and buys from him, then sells it." In general, the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade buying and selling whose kind is lawful, until the seller knows the price, which is the customary price, and the buyer knows the commodity.

The one who holds corrupt analogy (*qiyas fasid*) says: "The buyer may buy wherever he wishes, and he has bought from the seller, just as he says that he may act as agent for the resident seller and the non-resident seller." But the Lawgiver took into account the general interest, for if the importer does not know the price, he is ignorant of the customary price, so the buyer becomes a deceiver to him. Malik and Ahmad extended this to every *mustarsil* (one who is easily taken in in trade), for he is like the ignorant importer who does not know the price.

Thus it is clear that a person is obliged not to sell to such people except at the known price, which is the customary price, even if they are not in need of buying from him, because they are ignorant of the value, or do not bargain. Sale requires consent, and consent follows knowledge. Whoever does not know that it is a cheat may consent or may not consent. But if he knows that it is a cheat and consents, then there is no harm in it.

In the *Sunan* (of Abu Dawud): "A man had a tree on the land of another, and the landowner was harmed by the entry of the tree's owner. He complained of that to the Prophet (ﷺ), who commanded him to accept its exchange or to give it to him as a gift. He did not do so. So he permitted the landowner to uproot it, and said to the owner of the tree: 'You are only a harmer.'"

The one who holds corrupt analogy says: "He is not obliged to sell his tree, nor to give it away as a gift, nor is it permissible for the landowner to uproot it, because that is a disposal of another's property without his permission, and compulsion to exchange it." But the Lawgiver obliged him, if he would not give it as a gift, to sell it, because in that is the benefit of the landowner in being freed from the harm of the tree owner's entry, and the benefit of the tree owner in taking its value. Even if there is a slight harm to him in that, the harm to the landowner from its remaining in his orchard is greater. The Wise Lawgiver averts the greater of two harms by the lesser of them. This is jurisprudence, analogy, and the public interest, whoever refuses it.

The intent is this: this is evidence for the obligation of selling when the buyer is in need. And where is this from the general need of people for food and other things? The ruling on exchange of benefits, when people are in need of them, such as the benefit of houses, grinding, baking, and the like, is the ruling on exchange of goods.

The sum of the matter is this: when the people's interest cannot be completed except by fixing prices, then the ruler fixes prices for them at a just price, neither deficient nor excessive. And when their need is met and their interest is established without it, he does not do so. And success is from God.
